lessons.title: What “unexplained” means and the work-up behind it
lessons.objective: Define unexplained infertility as ESHRE does, complete the work-up that supports it, and recognise the tests that are not recommended.
lessons.closing: Unexplained is a diagnosis of exclusion after a complete basic work-up. More tests do not “explain” it: almost all additional tests carry a strong recommendation against.

lessons.title: Prognosis and first line: ESHRE versus NICE
lessons.objective: Decide between expectant management and active treatment by prognosis, know the evidence by outcome type, and explain why ESHRE and NICE differ.
lessons.closing: ESHRE: IUI with ovarian stimulation as first line, started according to prognosis. NICE: complete 2 years, then IUI with gonadotrophins or IVF. Neither supports stimulation alone.

lessons.title: Stimulated IUI and when to move to IVF
lessons.objective: Plan a safe stimulated IUI, individualise the move to IVF, avoid ICSI without a male factor, and not offer extras without proven benefit.
lessons.closing: Low dose and monitoring in IUI; IVF according to age, duration and previous treatment; conventional IVF without ICSI; and no scratching, antioxidants or inositol as an “extra”.

items.title: Unexplained: a diagnosis of exclusion
items.core: ESHRE defines unexplained infertility as infertility in couples with apparently normal ovarian function, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and pelvis, age ≤40 years (female partner) and adequate coital frequency, and with apparently normal testicular function, genito-urinary anatomy and a normal ejaculate. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
It is inevitably a diagnosis of exclusion after “standard” investigations, and the proportion of couples who receive it depends on how extensive those investigations are. ESHRE notes that about 30% of infertile couples are considered unexplained and acknowledges that there is still no consensus-standardised diagnostic work-up. As in the ICMART definition of infertility, at least 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse are required before investigations start. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

The guideline considers a cycle regular if it lasts 24–38 days, with bleeding of up to 8 days and a shortest-to-longest cycle variation below 7–9 days. If minimal to mild endometriosis is found incidentally at laparoscopy, ESHRE no longer considers it unexplained infertility. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

NICE speaks of “unexplained fertility problems” and offers both partners assessment after 1 year of unprotected intercourse when there is no known or suspected cause (1.16.5). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: According to ESHRE, what age limit and minimum time trying are part of the definition of unexplained infertility?
items.pearl: “Unexplained” describes the scope of the work-up done, not a proven cause: tell the couple exactly that.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Definition by the ESHRE 2023 guideline development group; NICE 2026.

items.title: What I would do: the work-up that supports the diagnosis
items.core: For ESHRE, the work-up includes the medical, reproductive and sexual history of both partners, at least one semen analysis according to WHO criteria, a tubal patency test (HSG or HyCoSy) and an ultrasound, preferably 3D, to exclude uterine anomalies. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
Semen analysis: in a laboratory with external quality control; if the first result is below the WHO lower fifth percentile reference limit (6th edition), repeat it after a 3-month interval. Tubes: HSG and HyCoSy are valid tests compared with laparoscopy and chromopertubation (strong; ⊕⊕⊕○) and comparable to each other. Uterus: ultrasound, preferably 3D (strong; ⊕○○○); MRI is not a first-line test (strong; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

Additions ESHRE does endorse: TSH and BMI as good pre-conception practice (GPP), and considering coeliac disease testing (conditional; ⊕⊕○○). With regular cycles there is no need to confirm ovulation routinely (GPP) or to measure ovarian reserve to identify the cause or predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong; ⊕⊕○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] NICE also suggests considering coeliac serology in unexplained subfertility (1.23.1). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: Which four components make up the work-up that, according to ESHRE, must be normal before calling infertility unexplained?

rows.text: ≥12 months of unprotected intercourse; woman ≤40 years
Medical, reproductive and sexual history of both
WHO semen analysis (repeat at 3 months if below the 5th percentile)
TSH and BMI (good practice); consider coeliac disease

visual.alt: Flow diagram: after at least 12 months without pregnancy and with the woman aged 40 or under, history of both partners, WHO semen analysis, HSG or HyCoSy for the tubes and ultrasound, preferably 3D, for the uterus. Note: TSH and BMI as good practice, and consider coeliac disease.

items.application: Before labelling a couple as unexplained, check that every step has been done; if one is missing, the diagnosis is provisional.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: strong recommendations with varying certainty (⊕○○○ to ⊕⊕⊕○), GPPs and one conditional (coeliac disease); NICE 2026.

items.title: What I would not order: uterus and pelvis with a normal ultrasound
items.core: If ultrasound assessment of the uterine cavity is normal, ESHRE recommends no further evaluation (strong; ⊕○○○), no routine diagnostic laparoscopy (strong; ⊕○○○) and no endometrial biopsy for histology without another indication (strong; ⊕⊕○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
It also does not recommend hysteroscopy to detect and correct intrauterine abnormalities not seen at routine imaging (strong; ⊕⊕○○): the available trials are at serious risk of bias and, in first IVF cycles, there was no significant difference in live birth (RR 1.20; 95% CI 0.96–1.49; 2 RCTs, 953 women). It does not recommend the post-coital test (strong; ⊕⊕○○) and suggests not routinely measuring mid-luteal progesterone with regular cycles (conditional; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

The laparoscopy recommendation was debated: HSG and HyCoSy do not detect mild endometriosis, adhesions or subtle tubal lesions, but there are insufficient data that omitting laparoscopy misses clinically relevant diagnoses in low-risk women. ESHRE advises counselling women at high tubal risk (previous PID or ectopic pregnancy) or with endometriosis about its benefits and risks. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] NICE agrees on not offering hysteroscopy unless a uterine or endometrial abnormality is clinically suspected (1.18.16). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: With a normal uterine ultrasound in unexplained infertility, what does ESHRE say about hysteroscopy, laparoscopy and endometrial biopsy?
items.application: With a history of PID, ectopic pregnancy or endometriosis symptoms, the laparoscopy conversation changes: she is no longer the low-risk patient the recommendation addresses.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: strong recommendations against (very low to low certainty) and one conditional against (luteal progesterone); NICE 2026.

items.title: What I would not order: normal semen analysis and systemic tests
items.core: With a normal semen analysis by WHO criteria, ESHRE does not recommend testing sperm DNA fragmentation, anti-sperm antibodies in semen or testicular imaging (all strong; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
With a normal semen analysis it also does not recommend sperm chromatin condensation, sperm aneuploidy screening, HPV or microbiology testing of semen, nor serum hormone testing (strong; ⊕○○○); seminal oxidative stress is for research only. In the systemic evaluation it does not recommend serum anti-sperm antibodies, thyroid antibodies or other autoimmune testing (apart from coeliac disease), thrombophilia testing, genetic or genomic tests, vitamin D for diagnosis or prolactin (strong; ⊕○○○), nor oxidative stress in women (strong; ⊕⊕○○). With a normal TSH, no additional thyroid evaluation is recommended (strong; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

ESHRE explains that these tests discriminate poorly between couples who would benefit from each technique, use heterogeneous and unvalidated cut-offs, and have no proven value for decision-making; it also acknowledges that the evidence is of very low quality and that the male factor is under-researched. NICE simply advises not testing sperm DNA fragmentation (1.17.6). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: With a normal semen analysis and normal TSH, name four tests ESHRE does not recommend in unexplained infertility.
items.application: Faced with a “complete” test bundle, the useful question is whether the result would change treatment; for this list, ESHRE concludes this has not been shown.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: strong recommendations against, almost all with very low certainty; NICE 2026.

items.title: Immunological tests and add-ons: do not mix scales
items.core: In assisted reproduction, ESHRE does not recommend peripheral blood tests for immune parameters or uterine NK-cell testing, and rates screening hysteroscopy as “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body:
The good practice document on add-ons uses four phrases: “recommended”; “can be considered”; “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” (not to be applied routinely at this stage; this may change with more evidence and, optionally, it can be applied to a specific patient group); and “not recommended” (because of safety concerns, lack of efficacy or lack of biological rationale; research settings only). Sperm DNA damage testing, endometrial scratching and KIR/HLA genotyping sit in the third category. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

Population and nuance: that document addresses patients in ART, and screening hysteroscopy “can be considered” in recurrent implantation failure. For couples with unexplained infertility, the specific guideline is firmer: hysteroscopy not recommended (strong; ⊕⊕○○) and fragmentation testing not recommended with a normal semen analysis (strong; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: What is the difference between “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” and “not recommended” in the ESHRE add-ons document?
items.pearl: Always quote the source's own scale: “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” is not the same as “not recommended”, and neither is a GRADE rating.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023 (good practice, own 4-level scale) versus the ESHRE 2023 unexplained infertility guideline (GRADE-style strength and certainty).

items.stem: She is 33 and they have been trying for 15 months. Regular cycles, normal 3D ultrasound, patent tubes on HSG and a normal semen analysis by WHO criteria. He asks for a sperm DNA fragmentation test he read about online. What is appropriate?

options.text: Explain that, with a normal semen analysis, ESHRE does not recommend it (strong recommendation) and NICE advises against doing it.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE does not recommend fragmentation testing with a normal WHO semen analysis (strong; ⊕○○○) and NICE advises against it (1.17.6).

options.text: Order it, because an abnormal result would indicate ICSI.
options.why: The test is not recommended and, in unexplained infertility, ESHRE does not recommend ICSI over conventional IVF (strong).

options.text: Order it together with anti-sperm antibodies in semen to complete the work-up.
options.why: With a normal semen analysis, ESHRE does not recommend anti-sperm antibodies in semen either (strong; ⊕○○○).

options.text: Repeat the semen analysis after 3 months before deciding anything.
options.why: ESHRE advises a repeat after 3 months when the first result is below the WHO 5th percentile, not when it is normal.

items.explanation: With a normal semen analysis, additional sperm tests are not recommended in unexplained infertility: they have not been shown to change decisions or predict reproductive outcomes.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with unexplained infertility and a normal 3D ultrasound of the uterine cavity has been offered a hysteroscopy “to make the uterus perfect before IUI”. According to ESHRE, what is correct?

options.text: No further evaluation is needed; hysteroscopy for abnormalities not seen at imaging is not recommended (strong).
options.why: Correct: with a normal ultrasound no further evaluation is needed (strong; ⊕○○○) and diagnostic-operative hysteroscopy is not recommended (strong; ⊕⊕○○).

options.text: Do it, because in some series it finds lesions in more than one in ten women with a normal ultrasound.
options.why: ESHRE reports such findings (mostly polyps and septa) but no proven outcome benefit; that is why it does not recommend it.

options.text: Order a pelvic MRI to confirm a normal uterus.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend MRI as a first-line test to confirm normal uterine anatomy (strong; ⊕○○○).

options.text: Replace it with an endometrial biopsy for histology.
options.why: Endometrial biopsy for histology is not recommended without other indications (strong; ⊕⊕○○).

items.explanation: In unexplained infertility, a normal uterine ultrasound closes the cavity assessment; hysteroscopy is reserved for clinical suspicion.

items.stem: In a woman with unexplained infertility and a normal TSH, which of these tests do ESHRE (conditional recommendation) and NICE (consider) allow for?

options.text: Coeliac serology.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE says it can be considered (conditional; ⊕⊕○○) and NICE suggests considering it (1.23.1).

options.text: Thyroid antibodies.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend thyroid antibodies or other autoimmune tests apart from coeliac disease (strong; ⊕○○○), nor further thyroid evaluation with a normal TSH.

options.text: Thrombophilia testing.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend thrombophilia testing in unexplained infertility (strong; ⊕○○○).

options.text: Prolactin.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend prolactin testing (strong; ⊕○○○) and NICE only offers it with an ovulatory disorder, galactorrhoea or a pituitary tumour (1.18.11).

items.explanation: Coeliac disease is the only exception ESHRE makes to its strong recommendation against autoimmune testing in unexplained infertility, and NICE agrees on considering it.

items.title: Decide by prognosis, not by label
items.core: ESHRE advises basing the decision to start active treatment on prognosis (GPP); the most important prognostic factors are age, duration of infertility, previous treatment and previous pregnancy. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
Models such as Hunault's estimate the chance of spontaneous pregnancy, but none is fully evolved: Hunault's was validated only in Canadian and Dutch populations and can be used only once, at diagnosis; newer dynamic models, initially validated in Dutch and Scottish populations, are not yet in common use. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

The guideline shows why efficacy “depends”: one RCT in couples with a favourable prognosis (intermediate, per the trial title, Steures 2006) found no difference in live birth between ovarian stimulation with IUI and expectant management, while another, in poor-prognosis couples, found a striking benefit of treatment. In young women with a short duration of infertility the added benefit is small; with older age and longer duration, it increases. The couple's preferences also count. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: Which four prognostic factors does ESHRE highlight for deciding when to start treatment in unexplained infertility?
items.pearl: Before discussing techniques, place the couple on their four prognostic factors: age, time trying, previous pregnancies and previous treatment.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: good practice point (GPP), based on a prognosis section added after stakeholder review.

items.title: Expectant versus active: what beats waiting
items.core: ESHRE recommends IUI with ovarian stimulation as first-line treatment for unexplained infertility (strong recommendation; very low certainty, ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
Against expectant management, the guideline summarises: clomiphene with timed intercourse was not better (cumulative birth rate 13% versus 16% with 6 months of expectant management; 1 RCT, 385 couples), and natural-cycle IUI showed no significant difference in live birth (23% versus 16%). No RCTs were found of letrozole or gonadotrophins with timed intercourse versus expectant management. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

Stimulated IUI versus expectant management (Cochrane review cited by ESHRE): with poor prognosis, OR for cumulative live birth 4.48 (95% CI 2.00–10.01; 1 RCT, 201 women); with moderate prognosis, OR for live birth 0.82 (0.45–1.49; 1 RCT, 253 women). Compared with natural-cycle IUI, stimulated IUI increased live birth (OR 2.07; 1.22–3.50; 4 RCTs, 396 women). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: Which options did not beat expectant management in the data ESHRE summarises, and in which prognosis did stimulated IUI do so?
items.pearl: Watch the outcome and the population: these are live birth and cumulative live birth data, and the benefit of stimulated IUI depends on baseline prognosis.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: strong recommendation with very low certainty; few, small trials per comparison.

items.title: ESHRE versus NICE: same couple, different timeline
items.core: NICE advises trying to conceive for a total of 2 years of regular unprotected intercourse before treatment (1.38.1); after that, consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophin ovarian stimulation before IVF, or offer IVF (1.38.3). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
ESHRE's recommendations do not set that second year: they recommend stimulated IUI as first line (strong; ⊕○○○), deciding when to start on prognosis (GPP), and consider that IVF is probably not recommended over stimulated IUI (conditional; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

Why they differ: NICE relied on a network meta-analysis and an NHS economic model that placed IVF as the most cost-effective first-line treatment; IUI with a gonadotrophin could be cost effective and is accepted as an alternative first-line option before IVF; the committee also acknowledged that some people may prefer the less invasive option. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] ESHRE argues that, in treatment-naïve patients, IVF is as effective as stimulated IUI and that the latter is considerably less invasive and costly. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: How long in total does NICE ask couples to try before treating unexplained infertility, and which two options does it offer afterwards?

rows.text: Unexplained infertility after ≥12 months and a normal work-up
ESHRE: by prognosis → stimulated IUI first line (strong, ⊕○○○)
NICE: keep trying to 2 years in total → up to 4 IUI with gonadotrophins, or IVF

visual.alt: Flow diagram: for unexplained infertility after at least 12 months and a normal work-up, ESHRE recommends deciding by prognosis and starting stimulated IUI as first line; NICE advises continuing to try until 2 years in total and then considering up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offering IVF. Note: neither supports ovarian stimulation alone.

items.application: Explain to the couple that the difference is one of timeline and criteria (NHS cost-effectiveness versus invasiveness and cost), not that one guideline is wrong.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Genuine guideline discrepancy: ESHRE 2023 (European, GRADE) versus NICE 2026 (UK, with an economic model).

items.title: Myth: “a few cycles of clomiphene or letrozole to help”
items.core: NICE advises not offering ovarian stimulation as a stand-alone treatment for unexplained fertility problems (1.38.2): its analysis found it neither effective nor cost effective. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
ESHRE reaches a similar conclusion in the justification of its recommendations, not as a formal recommendation: clomiphene, letrozole, gonadotrophins or IUI on their own are not effective compared with expectant management or natural-cycle IUI. For letrozole and gonadotrophins with timed intercourse it found no RCTs against expectant management, so that part is the development group's judgement. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

Between letrozole and clomiphene with timed intercourse, one RCT (172 women) found no difference in ongoing pregnancy, and another (270 women) found more clinical pregnancies with letrozole (23.07% versus 10.68%) and more multiple pregnancies with clomiphene. The guideline reports no live birth data for this comparison and makes no recommendation on which drug to use. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: What does NICE say about ovarian stimulation without IUI in unexplained infertility?
items.pearl: More clinical pregnancies in a small RCT do not equal more live births: that outcome is not reported for this comparison.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: NICE 2026 (explicit recommendation against); ESHRE 2023 (conclusion in the justification, not a formal recommendation).

items.title: Oil-based HSG: more than a test
items.core: ESHRE considers HSG (tubal flushing) with oil-soluble contrast preferable to water-soluble contrast and asks that its risks and benefits be discussed with all couples with unexplained infertility (conditional; ⊕⊕○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
In the meta-analysis cited, oil-based contrast probably increases clinical pregnancy compared with water-based contrast (OR 1.42; 95% CI 1.10–1.85; 6 RCTs, 2598 women); live birth was reported in 3 RCTs, two favouring oil and one showing no difference. In the 5-year follow-up of the largest trial (1119 women) there were more live births with oil-based contrast (RR 1.11; 1.03–1.20) and a shorter time to ongoing pregnancy. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

Risks: intravasation is more frequent with oil-based contrast (OR 5.00; 2.25–11.12), with no difference in infection or haemorrhage; four cases of serious embolism have been reported since 1928, so ESHRE stresses performing HSG under fluoroscopic control (the guideline says “fluorescence guidance”) so that it can be stopped in time. Part of the evidence comes from ovulatory women with diagnoses other than unexplained infertility, although, according to ESHRE, the largest trial (1119 women) included women with unexplained infertility. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: Which HSG contrast does ESHRE prefer in unexplained infertility, with what strength, and what is its main risk?
items.pearl: If HSG is already indicated, the type of contrast deserves a conversation with the couple, not just a technical choice.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: conditional recommendation (⊕⊕○○); requires shared decision-making.

items.stem: How does ESHRE 2023 grade its recommendation of IUI with ovarian stimulation as first line in unexplained infertility?

options.text: Strong, with very low certainty of evidence (⊕○○○).
options.why: Correct: it is a strong recommendation supported by very low certainty evidence; strength and certainty are different things.

options.text: Strong, with high certainty (⊕⊕⊕⊕).
options.why: None of this guideline's recommendations is supported by high-quality evidence.

options.text: Conditional, with low certainty (⊕⊕○○).
options.why: The recommendation is strong; the conditional one with ⊕○○○ is that IVF is probably not recommended over stimulated IUI.

options.text: A good practice point, with no evidence graded.
options.why: It is an evidence-based recommendation; the related good practice point is deciding when to start based on prognosis.

items.explanation: ESHRE separates strength of recommendation from certainty of evidence: a recommendation can be strong even when certainty is very low, and that is worth explaining to the couple.

items.stem: Couple seen in the NHS (UK); she is 31. After 12 months without pregnancy, the full work-up is normal. According to NICE NG257, what is appropriate now?

options.text: Advise them to keep trying until 2 years of regular unprotected intercourse in total before treatment.
options.why: Correct: NICE advises a total of 2 years before treatment (1.38.1).

options.text: Clomiphene with timed intercourse for 6 cycles.
options.why: NICE advises against ovarian stimulation as a stand-alone treatment (1.38.2).

options.text: Immediate IVF.
options.why: For unexplained infertility, NICE offers IVF after 2 years without conceiving, with or without IUI (1.39.3).

options.text: IUI with gonadotrophin stimulation starting now.
options.why: NICE positions stimulated IUI for those who have already tried for 2 years (1.38.3); this would be closer to ESHRE, which decides timing by prognosis.

items.explanation: NICE structures treatment of unexplained infertility over time: 2 years in total, then up to 4 IUI cycles with gonadotrophins, or IVF.

items.stem: In the 385-couple RCT in unexplained infertility summarised by ESHRE, what did clomiphene with timed intercourse show compared with 6 months of expectant management?

options.text: It did not improve the outcome: cumulative birth rate 13% versus 16% with expectant management.
options.why: Correct: that is ESHRE's summary, which also found no cost benefit of clomiphene over expectant management.

options.text: It doubled the live birth rate.
options.why: There was no benefit; the numerically higher figure was in the expectant group.

options.text: It increased clinical pregnancy, but the trial did not measure live birth.
options.why: The trial reported cumulative births and time to a pregnancy leading to live birth, with no advantage for clomiphene.

options.text: It improved cumulative live birth only in poor-prognosis couples.
options.why: That poor-prognosis benefit belongs to IUI with ovarian stimulation, not to clomiphene with timed intercourse.

items.explanation: Oral stimulation with timed intercourse does not beat waiting in unexplained infertility; what ESHRE recommends is IUI combined with stimulation.

items.title: What I would do: stimulated IUI with a low dose and monitoring
items.core: To avoid multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), ESHRE advises using gonadotrophins for IUI only in a low-dose regimen with adequate monitoring (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
In its justification, ESHRE regards IUI in a stimulated cycle for three to six cycles as first line, with low-dose gonadotrophins to avoid a high number of growing follicles; according to the latest European studies, a low dose greatly reduces multiple pregnancy without significantly reducing live birth. Compared with expectant management, the OR for multiple pregnancy with stimulated IUI was 3.01 (95% CI 0.47–19.28; 2 RCTs), a very wide interval. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

NICE positions up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins before IVF (1.38.3) and asks that ovulation induction or ovarian stimulation agents be limited to the lowest effective dose and duration (1.54.3). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What measure does ESHRE propose to reduce multiple pregnancy and OHSS in stimulated IUI, and how many cycles do ESHRE and NICE envisage?
items.application: When planning IUI, agree in advance with the couple how many cycles you will do and what will happen if the response is multifollicular.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: GPP; 3–6 cycles in ESHRE's justification versus “up to 4” in the NICE 2026 recommendation.

items.title: When to move to IVF?
items.core: ESHRE considers that IVF is probably not recommended over IUI with ovarian stimulation (conditional; ⊕○○○) and expects the decision to be individualised by age, duration of infertility, previous treatment and previous pregnancy (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
In the meta-analysis cited (8 RCTs), live birth was higher with IVF than with stimulated IUI (RR 1.54; 95% CI 1.04–2.28; 7 RCTs, 1391 women), with no significant difference in multiple pregnancy or OHSS. In treatment-naïve women under 38 there was no difference (RR 1.01; 0.88–1.15; 3 RCTs, 925 women); from 38 onwards it favoured IVF (RR 2.15; 1.16–4.00; a single RCT, 154 women). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

NICE offers IVF before the 42nd birthday to people with unexplained fertility problems who have not conceived after 2 years of regular unprotected intercourse, with or without IUI (1.39.3): 3 full cycles under 40, with up to 3 more considered (1.39.6, 1.39.7), and 1 full cycle at 40–41 if they have not had IVF before (1.39.9). A full cycle comprises one episode of ovarian stimulation and the transfer of all resulting fresh and frozen embryos (1.39.4). That 42nd-birthday limit is an access criterion for NHS-funded IVF, not a definition: it does not contradict the ≤40-year limit in ESHRE's definition. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: Which subgroup showed no live birth difference between IVF and stimulated IUI in the data ESHRE summarises?
items.pearl: The 38-and-over finding rests on a single RCT: it is an argument for individualising earlier, not a validated cut-off.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: conditional (⊕○○○) + GPP; NICE 2026: NHS access criteria based on an economic analysis.

items.title: What I would not do: “just in case” ICSI without a male factor
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend ICSI over conventional IVF in couples with unexplained infertility (strong; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
In the RCTs reviewed, live birth was similar: 35.5% with IVF versus 36.7% with ICSI in a subgroup of 382 couples (RR 1.03; 95% CI 0.79–1.35), and 46.7% versus 50% in an RCT of 60 couples. ESHRE adds the evidence of no difference in non-male factor infertility and the greater resources and costs of ICSI. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

NICE advises not using ICSI for non-male factor fertility problems if semen parameters are normal (1.50.3) and considering it with abnormal semen or previous failed fertilisation (1.50.2). The ESHRE add-ons document also rates ICSI for non-male factor infertility as “not recommended”. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.recall: When does NICE consider ICSI, and why is it not recommended in unexplained infertility?
items.application: If the couple asks for ICSI “to be sure”, separate two questions: whether there is an indication (abnormal semen, previous failed fertilisation) and whether it improves live birth without one (it does not).

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: strong against (⊕○○○); NICE 2026; ESHRE add-ons 2023 (not recommended).

items.title: What I would not offer as an “extra help”
items.core: ESHRE states that endometrial scratching should not be offered for unexplained infertility (strong; ⊕⊕○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
In the most recent RCT with timed intercourse (220 women), live birth was 9% versus 7% with a sham procedure (OR 1.39; 95% CI 0.50–4.03); overall, ESHRE concludes that the evidence does not show better pregnancy outcomes when scratching is performed before intercourse or IUI, although a few small individual RCTs did report more pregnancies. ESHRE also considers adjunct oral antioxidants in women and men (conditional; ⊕○○○), acupuncture in women (conditional; ⊕⊕○○) and inositol in women (conditional; ⊕○○○) probably not recommended. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

What it does endorse as good practice: psychological support, including psychotherapy, when needed, and a healthy diet with regular exercise, supported by behavioural therapy when necessary (GPP). NICE also does not offer scratching or hysteroscopy as pre-treatment to improve IVF outcomes (1.40.1, 1.40.2). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: How strongly does ESHRE advise against endometrial scratching, and how strongly against antioxidants and inositol, in unexplained infertility?
items.application: From an integrative perspective, the space ESHRE does support in this indication is lifestyle and psychological support, not antioxidants or inositol.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: scratching, strong against (⊕⊕○○); antioxidants, acupuncture and inositol, conditional against; lifestyle and psychological support, GPP. NICE 2026.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman; 3 years of unexplained infertility, no previous treatment. Which statement about IVF versus stimulated IUI is most faithful to ESHRE 2023?

options.text: IVF is probably not recommended over stimulated IUI (conditional), but the decision is individualised by age, duration and history; from 38 onwards, a single RCT favoured IVF.
options.why: Correct: it combines the conditional recommendation, the GPP on individualising and the subgroup finding with its limitation.

options.text: ESHRE recommends first-line IVF from age 38 (strong recommendation).
options.why: ESHRE makes no age-based recommendation; the 38-year finding comes from a single RCT within a sensitivity analysis.

options.text: IVF does not increase live birth over stimulated IUI in any analysis.
options.why: In the overall analysis live birth was higher with IVF (RR 1.54); equivalence was seen in treatment-naïve women under 38.

options.text: Because of her age, IVF with ICSI is recommended.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend ICSI over conventional IVF in unexplained infertility (strong), and age is not an ICSI indication in these guidelines.

items.explanation: The general recommendation favours starting with stimulated IUI, but ESHRE asks for individualisation: age, duration and history can justify IVF, with subgroup evidence that is still limited.

items.stem: A couple with unexplained infertility is about to start IVF; the semen analysis is normal. They ask for ICSI “to make sure of fertilisation”. What is appropriate?

options.text: Conventional IVF, explaining that ICSI is not recommended in this situation.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE does not recommend ICSI over conventional IVF in unexplained infertility (strong; ⊕○○○) and NICE advises against it with normal semen (1.50.3).

options.text: ICSI, because it increases live birth in unexplained infertility.
options.why: The RCTs reviewed by ESHRE show similar live birth (for example, 35.5% versus 36.7%).

options.text: ICSI, adding IMSI to select the sperm better.
options.why: Besides ICSI not being indicated, NICE advises against IMSI as an adjunct to ICSI (1.50.4).

options.text: Decide based on a sperm DNA fragmentation test.
options.why: With a normal semen analysis, ESHRE does not recommend that test (strong) and NICE advises against it (1.17.6).

items.explanation: Without a male factor or previous failed fertilisation, ICSI adds cost and resources without improving live birth in unexplained infertility.

items.stem: Before her first stimulated IUI, a patient with unexplained infertility asks about the “endometrial scratch” recommended on a forum. What is correct according to ESHRE?

options.text: It should not be offered (strong recommendation): overall, the evidence with timed intercourse and with IUI does not show better pregnancy outcomes.
options.why: Correct: “should not be offered for unexplained infertility” (strong; ⊕⊕○○).

options.text: It is recommended in the luteal phase of the cycle before IUI.
options.why: Timing varied between trials, but none justified recommending it; the recommendation is against.

options.text: It is probably not recommended (conditional), but it is a reasonable option if the patient wishes.
options.why: The strength is strong, not conditional; the conditional recommendations against are antioxidants, acupuncture and inositol.

options.text: It is only useful with timed intercourse, not before IUI.
options.why: In the most recent RCT with timed intercourse, live birth was 9% versus 7%, with no significant difference.

items.explanation: Scratching is a cheap outpatient procedure, but in unexplained infertility the evidence shows no benefit and ESHRE strongly advises against it.

items.stem: What does ESHRE propose to limit multiple pregnancy and OHSS in stimulated IUI for unexplained infertility?

options.text: Use gonadotrophins only in a low-dose regimen, with adequate monitoring.
options.why: Correct: this is ESHRE's good practice point accompanying the stimulated IUI recommendation.

options.text: Replace gonadotrophins with clomiphene.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend a specific drug, and in one cited RCT with timed intercourse (not IUI) multiple pregnancy was higher with clomiphene than with letrozole.

options.text: Use natural-cycle IUI as first line.
options.why: Natural-cycle IUI did not beat expectant management, and stimulated IUI increased live birth compared with it (OR 2.07).

options.text: Avoid IUI and move straight to IVF in all couples.
options.why: ESHRE considers IVF probably not recommended over stimulated IUI (conditional) and asks for individualisation.

items.explanation: The safety of stimulated IUI depends mainly on dose and monitoring: fewer growing follicles, less risk of multiple pregnancy.

items.title: Case: Ana, Tomás and “test us for everything”

steps.text: Ana (fictional case), 34, no previous pregnancies, regular 27–31-day cycles, no history of PID and no endometriosis symptoms. Tomás, 36. They have been trying for 14 months. Work-up: normal 3D ultrasound, patent tubes on HSG, normal WHO semen analysis and normal TSH. They arrive with a list: sperm DNA fragmentation, NK cells, hysteroscopy and thyroid antibodies.

Diagnosis and list: they meet the ESHRE definition (≤40 years, ≥12 months, normal basic work-up). With a normal semen analysis, ESHRE does not recommend DNA fragmentation testing (strong) and NICE advises against it.

With a normal ultrasound, hysteroscopy is not recommended (strong). Thyroid antibodies with a normal TSH are not recommended either (strong), and the ESHRE add-ons document does not recommend NK testing in ART. The only test ESHRE does allow considering here is coeliac serology.

Prognosis and timeline: Ana is young and has been trying for just over 1 year. ESHRE advises deciding when to start based on prognosis and recommends stimulated IUI as first line; NICE (guidance for the UK health system) would advise them to complete 2 years before treatment (1.38.1). You explain both positions and their reasons; per NICE, a miscarriage during that waiting period would not restart the clock (1.16.7). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

Shared decision: after a few more months, they choose stimulated IUI. It is planned with low-dose gonadotrophins and monitoring, agreeing in advance on the number of cycles (ESHRE envisages 3–6 in the justification of its recommendation; NICE, up to 4 before IVF) and what to do with a multifollicular response.

Twist: after 3 cycles without pregnancy, Ana asks about endometrial scratching, antioxidants and inositol. ESHRE strongly advises against scratching and considers antioxidants and inositol probably not recommended; it does endorse psychological support and healthy habits.
Move to IVF: weighing age, duration and previous treatment, the couple decide to move to IVF. With a normal semen analysis, conventional IVF will be used, not ICSI.

Communication: explain that “unexplained” reflects the limit of the work-up, not a failure of the couple; that more tests would not have changed the plan; and offer psychological support when they need it.

eshre-2023-addons.title: Good practice recommendations on add-ons in reproductive medicine
eshre-2023-addons.authors: ESHRE Add-ons Working Group; Lundin K, Bentzen JG, Bozdag G, Ebner T, Harper J, Le Clef N, Moffett A, Norcross S, Polyzos NP, Rautakallio-Hokkanen S, Sfontouris I, Sermon K, Vermeulen N, Pinborg A
eshre-2023-addons.population: Patients undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART); Hum Reprod 2023 (ESHRE Pages).
eshre-2023-addons.finding: 42 recommendations using its own four-phrase scale (recommended; can be considered; currently not recommended for routine clinical use; not recommended). Peripheral blood immune tests and uterine NK-cell testing: not recommended. Screening hysteroscopy: currently not recommended for routine clinical use (can be considered in recurrent implantation failure). Sperm DNA damage testing, endometrial scratching and KIR/HLA genotyping: currently not recommended for routine clinical use. ICSI for non-male factor infertility: not recommended.
eshre-2023-addons.limitations: Full text read (UCL Discovery open-access copy of the advance online version); the wording of every cited recommendation and the scale-definition table were checked verbatim. Good practice recommendations based on review and consensus, not a GRADE guideline: no recommendation rests on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence. ART population, not specifically unexplained infertility.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.
